facts.text: Trailer brakes are required above a 2,000-lb. trailer weight on Silverado, Suburban and Tahoe, and above a 1,500-lb. trailer weight on all other models (brake requirements vary by state; consult state laws).

An electric trailer brake system uses a brake control unit mounted inside the trailering vehicle; surge brakes are a self-contained hydraulic brake system on the trailer, activated during deceleration as the coupler pushes on the hitch ball.

If you'll be towing a trailer that requires a weight-distributing hitch, use a frame-mounted, weight-distributing hitch and sway control of the proper size (footnote: not required on Silverado 2500 HD or 3500 HD).
A weight-distributing hitch distributes the trailer tongue load by using spring bars to shift some of the hitch weight forward onto the tow vehicle's front axle and rearward to the trailer's axles.
Conventional hitch: a hitch ball mounted to a receiver or step bumper; the ball diameter must match the trailer coupler and the ball must meet or exceed the gross trailer weight rating.

Gooseneck and fifth-wheel hitches must be attached to the truck frame (not supported by the pickup bed) and mounted so the kingpin load is near the rear axle centerline; kingpin loads are higher than conventional tongue loads, so watch payload and RGAWR.

Trailer classes: Light-Duty (I) up to 2,000 lbs, conventional hitch; Medium-Duty (II) 2,001-3,500 lbs, conventional hitch; Heavy-Duty (III) 3,501-5,000 lbs, conventional or weight-distributing hitch; Extra Heavy-Duty (IV) 5,001-10,000 lbs and Maximum Heavy-Duty (V) 10,001 lbs and above, conventional, weight-distributing, fifth-wheel or gooseneck hitch (minimum recommended hitch).

Addition of trailer hitch weight cannot cause vehicle weights to exceed the Rear Gross Axle Weight Rating (RGAWR) or Gross Vehicle Weight Rating (GVWR); these ratings are on the certification label on the driver door or doorframe. GVW includes the vehicle, driver, passengers, fuel, optional equipment and cargo.

GCWR (Gross Combination Weight Rating) is the total allowable weight of the completely loaded vehicle and trailer; it is on the Trailering Information Label on the doorframe for Silverado 1500, Silverado EV, Silverado HD, Suburban and Tahoe, or in the Owner's Manual.

Maximum trailer weight rating is determined by subtracting the tow vehicle's curb weight from the GCWR; base curb weight plus 150 lbs each for the driver and a front passenger is used, so additional passengers, equipment and cargo reduce the rating.
In general, a higher axle ratio offers higher trailer weight ratings, quicker acceleration and less fuel efficiency; a lower axle ratio offers more fuel efficiency but lower trailer weight ratings.
Tow ratings depend on driveline torque, powertrain cooling capacity, suspension and chassis load capacity, and stability items such as tire grip, wheelbase and steering response.

The maximum trailer weight rating is calculated for a line of vehicles assuming a driver, a front-seat passenger and all required trailering equipment; it may be necessary to reduce trailer weight to stay within GCWR, GVWR, maximum trailer tongue load or RGAWR.

Tongue weight should be 10% to 15% of the loaded trailer weight for conventional trailering and 15% to 25% for gooseneck/fifth-wheel trailering; when towing the maximum trailer weight, the maximum tongue weight is 10% for conventional and 15% for gooseneck/fifth-wheel trailers.
The GVWR is the maximum the vehicle itself should weigh, including as-equipped vehicle weight plus cargo, passengers and trailer tongue weight.
The only way to be sure not to exceed GCWR, GVWR, RGAWR or trailer weight rating is to weigh the fully loaded tow vehicle and trailer combination.

Load a conventional trailer to a 10% to 15% tongue weight (some trailer types, especially boat trailers, fall outside this range; follow the trailer Owner's Manual); with centered axles, put about 60% of the load over the front half of the trailer.

The Trailering Information Label on the driver-side door jamb lists GVWR, GCWR, rear GAWR (Gross Axle Weight Rating), maximum payload, maximum tongue weight and curb weight; included on Silverado 1500, Silverado EV, Silverado HD, Suburban and Tahoe.
Gooseneck/fifth-wheel kingpin weight should be 15% to 25% of the total loaded trailer weight and cannot cause the vehicle to exceed RGAWR or GVWR.
